name: Yawa
confidence_why: Jones 1986 called Yawa stress contrastive but found no minimal pairs and could not state the rules by which it shifts with a word's grammatical context, and van Schie 2026, a full dissertation with acoustic data on three Yawa-Saweru varieties, reanalyses that shifting prominence as phrase-level intonation with no word stress at all, so the older lexical-stress coding is the weaker reading.

catalog_quote: The phonological word in Yawa is defined as a unit of one and only one primary stress. Long words may have secondary stress(es), but not necessarily. ... The predominant features of stress are intensity and high pitch. ... Stress is contrastive in Yawa in that the syllable on which it occurs is not predictable. Compare the following three nouns, where the stress (indicated by an accent) is on the first, second, and third syllables respectively: ánauja ma it's a garden, anáne ma it's sago, and anománe ma it's a pan. Despite the fact that stress is contrastive, like in most other Papuan languages, it does not carry a heavy functional load. There are no words that contrast solely by stress placement. audit.recode_to: No word-level stress (phrasal prominence only: in Ambaidiru/Central Yawa a final intonational phrase has a penultimate pitch-marked prominent syllable, a non-final phrase an ultimate pitch+length-marked one; Turu: falling ultima in final phrases, ultimate prominence in non-final), per van Schie 2026 §3.6 pp. 92-111; keep Jones 1986 'lexical/contrastive with unexplained perturbation' as the superseded earlier analysis in contra/caution. If the catalog will not reclassify on a dialect mismatch (van Schie measured Ambaidiru/Turu, Jones described Sarawandori), at minimum add a contra entry and caution and drop the grade of confidence in lexical.
audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: every fragment of the deciding quotation, the domain quote and the exception quote is on printed pp. 20-21, 23 and 27 of the Jones 1986 PDF we hold (page scan read; txt layer scanned-noisy but matching). (2) Deciding source: a 1986 30-pp. impressionistic phonology article on one village dialect (Sarawandori) after six months' fieldwork; Jones herself says stress has no functional load, no minimal pairs, shifts with grammatical function by rules she could not formulate, and (1991b) marks no word boundaries. sources.citation: van Schie, Anne. 2024. A new approach to Yawa-Saweru prosody. Abstract, ETT 2024 (ett2024.github.io/abstracts/), 1 p.
sources.quote: 'In Jones (1986), stress in Yawa Sarawandori is described as lexically determined and contrastive. However, Jones also mentions there is a considerable amount of stress perturbation ... The complexity and equivocation in these descriptions call into question the validity of a lexical stress analysis ... I will propose a new analysis of Yawa-Saweru prosody, arguing that there is no such thing as lexical stress in Yawa-Saweru. Rather ... what has before been perceived as lexical stress is actually the implementation of a strong phrasal intonation system in which each intonational phrase has a si
sources.note: One-page abstract that names Jones 1986 (Sarawandori) directly and argues its 'lexical stress + perturbation' is phrasal intonation; bridges van Schie's Ambaidiru/Turu measurements to the exact dialect our record rests on.
